questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: Federal law requires sellers of residential housing built before 1978 to disclose the possible presence of:

answers.text: lead-based paint and provide an EPA-approved information pamphlet
radon gas above EPA action levels
asbestos insulation in the attic
underground storage tanks on the property

explanations.a: The Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act requires sellers and landlords of pre-1978 housing to disclose known lead hazards and provide buyers with the EPA pamphlet 'Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home.'
explanations.b: Radon disclosure may be required under some state laws but is not the subject of the specific pre-1978 federal mandate.
explanations.c: Asbestos disclosure is not specifically mandated by the same federal residential disclosure statute as lead paint.
explanations.d: Underground storage tank disclosure requirements exist but are not the focus of the pre-1978 housing rule.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: The EPA recommends that homeowners take corrective action when indoor radon levels reach or exceed:

answers.text: 2 picocuries per liter (pCi/L)
4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L)
10 picocuries per liter (pCi/L)
25 picocuries per liter (pCi/L)

explanations.a: The EPA considers 2 pCi/L the average indoor level; action is not required at that level but mitigation is still suggested.
explanations.b: The EPA action level for radon is 4 pCi/L; at that concentration or above, the agency recommends mitigation to reduce health risk.
explanations.c: 10 pCi/L significantly exceeds the action level; intervention would already be strongly advisable at 4 pCi/L.
explanations.d: 25 pCi/L is far above the action level; the EPA standard has been 4 pCi/L.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: A seller's property condition disclosure form is intended primarily to:

answers.text: transfer liability for all defects from the seller to the buyer after closing
satisfy the lender's requirement for a professional property appraisal
inform buyers of known material defects so they can make an informed purchasing decision
replace the buyer's obligation to obtain an independent home inspection

explanations.a: A disclosure form does not automatically shift liability; concealment or misrepresentation can still expose the seller to claims.
explanations.b: Property condition disclosure is distinct from an appraisal; lenders require an appraisal, not a seller's disclosure form.
explanations.c: The purpose of mandatory seller disclosure is to give buyers information about the property's known condition so they can negotiate or decide whether to proceed.
explanations.d: A seller's disclosure supplements but does not replace a buyer's right to obtain an independent home inspection.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: A property was the site of a highly publicized murder three years ago. Whether a seller must disclose this fact to a buyer depends primarily on:

answers.text: federal Fair Housing Act requirements for psychological impact disclosures
state law, which varies widely on what stigmatizing events must be disclosed
RESPA regulations governing material transaction disclosures
the buyer's real estate agent, who must always volunteer known stigmatizing information

explanations.a: The federal Fair Housing Act addresses protected class discrimination, not psychological stigma disclosure.
explanations.b: Disclosure obligations for stigmatized properties — murders, suicides, alleged hauntings — vary widely by state statute; some states require disclosure, others explicitly exempt it.
explanations.c: RESPA governs settlement service procedures and cost disclosures, not stigmatizing event disclosures.
explanations.d: A buyer's agent owes duties to the client but is not universally required to disclose stigma events without a state law mandate.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: Real estate brokers who agree with competitors to divide markets by geographic area or customer type are engaging in:

answers.text: market allocation, a per se violation of federal antitrust law
cooperative marketing permissible under RESPA guidelines
designated agency, a recognized form of buyer and seller representation
an MLS participation agreement approved by the local association

explanations.a: Agreements among competitors to divide markets — whether by geography, client type, or property category — constitute market allocation, treated as a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act.
explanations.b: Cooperative marketing through legal channels such as the MLS is permissible; an agreement to divide markets is not.
explanations.c: Designated agency describes representation within one brokerage firm, not competitor agreements about market territory.
explanations.d: MLS participation agreements set data-sharing rules; they do not authorize competitors to allocate markets among themselves.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: A real estate company requires buyers who use its brokerage services to also use its affiliated title company. This practice may violate antitrust laws because it is:

answers.text: a tying arrangement that conditions one service on the purchase of another
a buyer agency agreement with an exclusive representation clause
a net listing that creates a conflict of interest with the buyer
permissible only if the title company is separately incorporated

explanations.a: A tying arrangement conditions the sale of a desired product or service on the purchase of a second product. Conditioning brokerage services on using an affiliated title company may violate antitrust law and also RESPA Section 9.
explanations.b: An exclusive buyer agency agreement restricts which broker the buyer works with, not which settlement service providers must be used.
explanations.c: A net listing relates to how the broker's compensation is calculated; it does not describe forced title company use.
explanations.d: Separate incorporation of the title company does not cure the antitrust or RESPA concern if the buyer is given no choice.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.keyword: Do Not Call Registry violation fines
questions.text: A real estate licensee who calls a consumer on the National Do Not Call Registry to solicit a listing is:

answers.text: permitted to call as long as the call occurs during daytime business hours
exempt because real estate services are not covered by the registry
required only to identify the brokerage firm at the beginning of the call
subject to fines and may be in violation of FTC regulations

explanations.a: The time of day does not create an exemption for contacting registered numbers.
explanations.b: Real estate solicitation calls are covered by the registry; there is no blanket exemption for the real estate industry.
explanations.c: Identifying the firm is a telemarketing requirement but does not permit calling a registered number.
explanations.d: Calling a number on the National Do Not Call Registry for solicitation purposes exposes the caller to FTC enforcement and fines of thousands of dollars per violation.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: A real estate broker may call a consumer on the Do Not Call Registry without violating the rules if the consumer:

answers.text: owns commercial rather than residential property
has given written consent or has an established business relationship within the allowed time frame
lives in a rural area not served by an active MLS
placed the property on the market at any point in the past five years

explanations.a: The Do Not Call rules apply based on the consumer's registration, not the property type.
explanations.b: The established business relationship exemption (generally 18 months from the last transaction or 3 months from an inquiry) and prior written consent both permit contact with registered numbers.
explanations.c: Geographic location and MLS availability are not exemptions under the Do Not Call rules.
explanations.d: Prior ownership or listing activity does not automatically create a current business relationship that permits calls.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: Under the CAN-SPAM Act, every commercial email sent by a real estate licensee must include:

answers.text: the broker's state license number in the subject line
the full text of the licensee's agency disclosure statement
an attachment confirming the sender's identity verified by the state commission
a clear and conspicuous way for recipients to opt out of future messages

explanations.a: The CAN-SPAM Act does not require a license number in the subject line.
explanations.b: Agency disclosure requirements exist under state real estate law; they are not a CAN-SPAM requirement.
explanations.c: There is no requirement for a state-verified identity attachment under CAN-SPAM.
explanations.d: The CAN-SPAM Act requires that every commercial email contain a clear, conspicuous, and functional mechanism for recipients to opt out of further commercial messages from the sender.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: The CAN-SPAM Act prohibits real estate licensees from sending commercial emails with subject lines that:

answers.text: contain the name of the sending brokerage firm
reference a property the licensee has listed in the MLS
are misleading or deceptive about the content of the email
exceed 75 characters in length

explanations.a: Including the brokerage name in the subject line is permitted and often required for identification.
explanations.b: Referencing a listed property in the subject line is permissible and not deceptive.
explanations.c: CAN-SPAM bars subject lines that deceive recipients about the email's content; all identifying information must be accurate.
explanations.d: CAN-SPAM does not impose a character limit on subject lines.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: A real estate agent who tells homeowners their neighborhood's racial composition is changing and urges them to sell quickly at reduced prices is engaging in:

answers.text: steering
redlining
blockbusting
churning

explanations.a: Steering directs buyers toward or away from certain areas based on protected characteristics; the scenario describes the agent targeting sellers.
explanations.b: Redlining is the practice by lenders of denying services in geographic areas based on racial composition.
explanations.c: Blockbusting (or panic peddling) is inducing owners to sell by suggesting that protected-class individuals are moving into the neighborhood, which is a federal Fair Housing Act violation.
explanations.d: Churning refers to excessive trading of investment accounts to generate commissions; it is not a real estate fair housing term.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: A licensee who shows buyers properties only in neighborhoods matching the buyers' race or national origin is engaging in:

answers.text: designated agency on the buyer's behalf
acceptable customer service by matching preferences to communities
blockbusting directed at the neighborhoods being avoided
steering, which violates the Fair Housing Act

explanations.a: Designated agency is a form of representation within a brokerage; it does not describe directing buyers based on protected characteristics.
explanations.b: Matching buyers to neighborhoods based on protected class characteristics is not acceptable customer service — it is illegal steering regardless of whether the buyer expressed a preference.
explanations.c: Blockbusting targets sellers by exploiting fears about neighborhood change; the conduct described here is steering, which targets buyers.
explanations.d: Steering is the illegal practice of directing buyers toward or away from specific areas based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, or disability.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.keyword: Fair Housing Act protected classes EXCEPT
questions.text: The federal Fair Housing Act of 1968, as amended, prohibits discrimination in housing based on all of the following EXCEPT:

answers.text: familial status
disability
national origin
occupation or profession

explanations.a: Familial status — having children under 18 in the household — is a federally protected class added by the 1988 Fair Housing Amendments Act.
explanations.b: Disability is a federally protected class under the 1988 amendments.
explanations.c: National origin has been a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act since its original enactment in 1968.
explanations.d: Occupation or profession is not a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act; a landlord may lawfully decline to rent based on a prospective tenant's profession.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: Under the Fair Housing Act, a landlord is generally required to allow a tenant with a disability to:

answers.text: pay a reduced security deposit as an accommodation
make reasonable modifications to the unit at the tenant's own expense
permanently alter common areas without landlord approval
keep any assistance animal with no pet deposit under any circumstances

explanations.a: The Fair Housing Act does not require landlords to reduce security deposits for tenants with disabilities.
explanations.b: A landlord must allow a tenant with a disability to make reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense, though the landlord may require restoration at lease end.
explanations.c: Modifications to common areas require landlord approval; a tenant may not unilaterally alter common areas.
explanations.d: While assistance animals must be accommodated, landlords may charge for actual damage caused; a blanket no-charge rule is an overstatement.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: A seller knows the property has a recurring mold problem, and the listing agent learns of it. The agent's duty requires:

answers.text: disclosing the known mold condition to prospective buyers as a material fact
concealing the condition to protect the seller's negotiating position
mentioning it only if the buyer's inspector specifically tests for mold
reporting the condition to the local health department before listing

explanations.a: Mold is a material condition affecting health and property value; both the seller and the listing agent have a duty to disclose known material defects to prospective buyers.
explanations.b: Concealment of a known material defect exposes both the seller and agent to misrepresentation claims and license law sanctions.
explanations.c: The duty to disclose is proactive; it does not depend on whether the buyer's inspector happens to test for mold.
explanations.d: No law generally requires reporting residential mold to the health department as a condition of listing; the duty is to disclose it to buyers.

questions.name: Marketing Regulations
questions.text: HUD fair housing advertising guidelines suggest that when human models appear in real estate marketing materials, the models should:

answers.text: represent only the demographic profile of the surrounding neighborhood
be exclusively of the same race as the target buyer audience
reflect a diversity of racial and ethnic backgrounds to signal openness to all protected classes
be omitted entirely from residential real estate advertising

explanations.a: Limiting models to the existing neighborhood's demographic could itself imply racial steering.
explanations.b: Using models of only one race signals that the housing is intended for that group, which violates fair housing advertising standards.
explanations.c: HUD's advertising guidelines encourage diverse human models across race, national origin, and other protected classes to communicate that the housing is open to all.
explanations.d: Using human models in advertising is permissible; omitters are not required, and advertisers are guided to include diverse representation.
